items.item: The hook's failure is about the gap between revocation and consumer cutover, not about rotation itself being risky — a learner who thinks 'rotate less' is the fix hasn't located the actual defect

at.step: What's the one change that prevents every one of those failures?

items.item: A dual-credential rotation only causes zero downtime if the old credential is cut on confirmed zero-usage, not on a fixed timer — a fixed timer just narrows the same race rather than closing it, which the prove-it step tests directly

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Dynamic roles and static roles in Vault solve genuinely different problems (per-consumer freshly-minted credentials vs. scheduled rotation of one shared existing user), not two names for the same feature

at.step: A credential that expires without anyone revoking it

items.item: An orchestrator's own metastore is an ordinary database from a security standpoint — anyone with read access to it can read whatever secret value was stored there directly, which is the actual reason task-time lookup against a real secrets backend matters

items.item: Each of the three never-commit surfaces fails differently, not identically: an image layer is distributed to every puller, a notebook commits by accident via its own output cells, and DAG code persists in version-control history independent of whether the current file still has it

at.step: Three surfaces, one mistake

items.item: A managed secret store's real value proposition is not 'storage' at all — access control, an audit trail and versioned rollback are the three things a plain environment variable or config file cannot provide at any price

items.item: The 'alternating users' pattern AWS documents for RDS generalizes to any database that supports creating a second role with identical grants — nothing about it is RDS-specific, which is why it reproduces faithfully against local PostgreSQL

at.step: Two roles, not one password, is the whole trick

items.item: Vault's own internals are sourced-only in this topic since Vault isn't installed locally; the dynamic-credential property demonstrated (self-expiring, no separate revoke) is reproduced with a different real mechanism (PostgreSQL's VALID UNTIL), which is disclosed, not presented as Vault itself running

A secrets backend being 'checked first' and 'non-configurable' in search order are two separate facts; the ordering guarantee is what prevents a stale metastore value from silently winning even when a secrets backend is enabled
